introduction-the-aws-vending-machine.core: Identity pools (federated identities) are a credential vending machine: present a valid identity (Cognito user pool token, Google, Apple, SAML, OIDC or none for guests) and receive temporary AWS credentials for an IAM role, letting browser and mobile apps call AWS services directly and securely.

first_principles.problem: A mobile app embeds long-lived AWS access keys to upload to S3, and they get extracted.
truths: Roles limit what credentials can do.

analogy.title: A vending machine that accepts verified tokens
analogy.story: Insert a valid token and get a limited-value card that expires soon.
analogy.breaks: Vending cards work anywhere; credentials only allow what the role permits.

example.title: No embedded keys
flow: Before: hard-coded access keys in app
Role allows only user's S3 prefix

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Extracted credentials are short-lived and narrow.

example.outcome: safe direct AWS access from clients.

check.a: Temporary AWS credentials for an IAM role.

authentication-vs-authorization-roles.core: Identity pools assign IAM roles: one for authenticated users, an optional one for unauthenticated (guest) users, and rule-based or token-based role mapping (e.g. from cognito:groups or preferred_role claims). The role's policies decide what AWS actions are allowed; authentication alone grants nothing.

first_principles.problem: All signed-in users get the same broad role, so regular users can access admin resources.
truths: Authentication proves identity; authorisation grants actions.
derivation: Trust policy restricts **identity pool ID and amr**.

analogy.title: Different coloured wristbands at a venue
analogy.story: Entry proves you have a ticket; the colour decides which areas you can enter.
analogy.breaks: Wristbands are fixed for the night; role mappings can change per session.

example.title: Group-based role mapping
example.outcome: correct authorisation for every user class.

check.q: What does the 'amr' condition in an identity pool role trust policy distinguish?
check.a: Whether the identity is authenticated or unauthenticated.

the-flow-from-app-to-s3.core: The flow: the user signs in to a user pool and gets an ID token; the app calls GetId with the token to get an identity ID, then GetCredentialsForIdentity to obtain temporary credentials (enhanced flow) for the mapped role; the SDK signs S3 requests with those credentials. Amplify and SDK credential providers automate this.

first_principles.problem: Developers are confused about how a login turns into permission to upload a file.
truths: Each step exchanges one proof for another.
Identity IDs are stable per user.

analogy.title: Checking into a hotel
analogy.story: Show ID at reception, get a room number, then a key card that opens your room until checkout.
analogy.breaks: Key cards don't renew themselves; SDK credential providers do.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Direct, signed upload with no backend.

check.q: Which API returns temporary credentials in the identity pool enhanced flow?

row-level-security-iam-policy-variables.core: IAM policy variables like ${cognito-identity.amazonaws.com:sub} insert the caller's identity ID into policies, so one role can restrict each user to their own S3 prefix or their own DynamoDB items (dynamodb:LeadingKeys). This gives per-user data isolation without per-user policies.

first_principles.problem: All authenticated users share a role that can read every user's files.
truths: Data can be keyed by identity.
derivation: Use **principal tags** (ABAC) for attributes like tenant.

analogy.title: Personal lockers opened by your own badge number
analogy.story: Every badge works on the locker with its own number only.
analogy.breaks: Lockers are physical; policy variables are evaluated per request.

example.title: Per-user S3 policy

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each user can only touch their own folder.

example.outcome: per-user isolation at the IAM layer.

check.q: How do you restrict a DynamoDB table to a user's own items via IAM?
check.a: Use the dynamodb:LeadingKeys condition with the identity ID policy variable as the partition key.

identity-pool-vs-user-pool-knowing-which.core: Use a user pool when you need sign-up, sign-in and tokens for your own APIs. Use an identity pool when clients must call AWS services directly with IAM credentials, including guest access or federated identities from other IdPs. Use both when signed-in users also need direct AWS access.

first_principles.problem: A team adds an identity pool just to protect its own API, when JWT authorizers would do.
derivation: **Guest AWS access** → identity pool unauthenticated role.
**External IdP to AWS** → identity pool federation.

analogy.title: A membership card versus a cash card
analogy.story: The membership card gets you into the club; the cash card lets you buy things from AWS's shop.
analogy.breaks: Cards are separate; identity pools usually accept user pool tokens to issue credentials.

branches.label: Anti-pattern
children: Identity pool to protect own API

example.title: Three scenarios
flow: Web app calling own REST API → user pool
Anonymous analytics to Kinesis → identity pool (guest)

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Match the tool to the target API.

check.q: Which pool do you need for guest users to send data directly to Kinesis?
check.a: An identity pool with an unauthenticated role.
